title: NOT NULL constraint
description: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL adds a NOT NULL constraint to a column that already exists - Postgres checks every current row first, so this fails if any row already has NULL there. This is why a real migration usually adds a new column with a DEFAULT (so existing rows are never NULL to begin with) before tightening it to NOT NULL. Add a `loyalty_tier` (TEXT) column to `customers` with a DEFAULT of `'standard'`, then add a NOT NULL constraint to that same column.
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: ALTER COLUMN, SET NOT NULL

Two statements: ADD COLUMN loyalty_tier TEXT DEFAULT 'standard' first (every existing row instantly gets 'standard', never NULL), then ALTER COLUMN loyalty_tier SET NOT NULL - which now succeeds because no row is NULL.
Write the ADD COLUMN statement with its DEFAULT, then a semicolon, then a second ALTER TABLE statement on the same table and column ending in SET NOT NULL.
expected_behavior: customers gains a loyalty_tier column, defaulted to 'standard' for existing rows, and now required (NOT NULL) going forward.
solution: ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN loyalty_tier TEXT DEFAULT 'standard'; ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN loyalty_tier SET NOT NULL;
explanation: SET NOT NULL is checked immediately against every existing row - adding the column WITH a DEFAULT first is what makes that check pass, since every row gets a real value the instant the column is added rather than NULL.
